I largely agree with your conclusion on this point. I'd point out that the American Experiment has always required flexibility and has evolved fairly well. Obviously, we began as an agrarian economy that had far more in common with our bronze-age ancestors than with modernity. Family farms and/or slave labor drove America during it's formative years. The industrial revolution upended the political structure and resulted in mass migration to cities (away from farms). Unchecked capitalism during that era resulted in egregious abuses (e.g. child labor, forced payment in worthless company script, dangerous working conditions, etc.). It also created the super-wealthy who brutally exercised undue influence over the political process. The resulting union-movement was a political reaction to those abuses and dominated the mid-20th Century. Now that we're in a post technological-revolution era, it remains to be seen how the dust will settle. Luckily, the Constitution is a pretty good document to under-gird our principles.

It should be noted that when it was written it was largely aspirational and that it took us about another century before we abolished slavery (All men being created equal and what not) and even longer to allow women to vote. But as a guiding document it points us in a good direction. Hopefully more people will come to understand that it is a living document that we can turn to while our socio-economic situation evolves. To anchor the Constitution to a rigid 18th Century interpretation will relegate the document (and our nation) to a backwards, unadaptable position that is unsustainable.
